target.title: Robust Self-Supervised Audio-Visual Speech Recognition
target.version: Interspeech 2022 proceedings version; no version label on first page
target.version_note: Read: Interspeech 2022 proceedings text (isca-shi22-robustav, DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2022-99). First public as arXiv:2201.01763 (2022-01; wiki arxiv-2201.01763 holds v3).

entries.text: The authors present a self-supervised AVSR framework built on AV-HuBERT, pretraining on unlabeled audio-visual speech before fine-tuning with transcribed data.
entries.condition: Framework novelty claim; AV-HuBERT joint audio-visual representations.
entries.quote: This paper presents a self-supervised framework for robust AVSR, which is based upon the recently introduced Audio- Visual HuBERT (AV-HuBERT) pre-training appraoch [18].

entries.text: The authors call this, to their knowledge, the first AVSR model built using a large volume of unlabeled audio-visual speech data.
entries.condition: Authors' qualified priority claim; no independent priority verification in the paper.
entries.quote: To our knowl- edge, this is the first attempt towards building an AVSR model using a large volume of unlabeled audio-visual speech data.

entries.text: The paper claims a new state of the art in audio-visual speech recognition and robustness to different noise categories.
entries.condition: Authors' conclusion for the evaluated LRS3 benchmark and noise tests.

entries.text: With 30h labeled fine-tuning, babble-noise average WER is 14.1% versus 28.0% for Xu et al. [15], a reported 49.6% relative reduction.
entries.condition: LRS3; babble noise; mean over SNR -10, -5, 0, 5, 10 dB; 30h labeled AV speech for AV-HuBERT versus Xu et al. [15] with 433h; Table 2 reports the model rows.

entries.text: The low-resource result uses 30h labels, less than 10% of the 433h mid-resource LRS3 labeled set.
entries.condition: Fine-tuning labels on LRS3; low-resource 30h compared with mid-resource 433h.

entries.text: For the 433h noise-augmented AV-HuBERT setup, average noisy WER falls from 25.8% for audio-only to 5.8% for audio-visual input, over 75% relative reduction.
entries.condition: LRS3; 433h labels; noisy conditions averaged over four noise types and five SNR levels in Table 3; noisy-pretrained LARGE model, audio-only versus audio-visual.

entries.text: The best clean-audio AV-HuBERT result is 1.4% WER versus 2.3% for Ma et al. [26], a reported 39.0% relative improvement, using fewer labeled hours (433h versus 595h).
entries.unit: % relative WER improvement; % WER; labeled hours
entries.condition: LRS3 clean test condition; AV input; AV-HuBERT uses 433h; Ma et al. [26] row lists 595h; Table 2.
entries.quote: our best model outperforms the best model from Ma et al. [26] by 39.0% (2.3%→1.4%) while using fewer labeled data.

entries.text: At 0dB babble SNR with 30h labels, AV-HuBERT reports 8.3% WER versus 42.5% for Afouras et al. [14], an 80.4% relative reduction.
entries.condition: LRS3 babble-noise evaluation at 0dB SNR; AV-HuBERT uses 30h labels; Afouras et al. [14] baseline.

entries.text: At 0dB babble SNR with 30h labels, AV-HuBERT reports 8.3% WER versus 25.5% for Xu et al. [15], a 67.4% relative reduction.
entries.condition: LRS3 babble-noise evaluation at 0dB SNR; AV-HuBERT uses 30h labels; Xu et al. [15] baseline uses 433h per Table 2.

entries.text: Across babble SNRs, the 30h AV-HuBERT model reports 14.1% average WER versus 28.0% for Xu et al. [15] (433h), a 49.6% relative reduction.
entries.condition: LRS3 babble; mean across -10, -5, 0, 5, 10 dB; 30h AV-HuBERT versus 433h Xu et al. [15].
entries.quote: Compared to the former SOTA [15], we achieve 49.6% lower WER (28.0% →14.1%) on average across different SNR ratios with 10 times fewer labels.

entries.text: With 433h labeled fine-tuning, average babble WER is 12.4% versus 28.0% for Xu et al. [15], a reported 55.7% relative improvement.
entries.condition: LRS3 babble; mean over five SNR levels; 433h AV-HuBERT versus Xu et al. [15] with 433h.

entries.text: For noise types beyond babble, the authors report over 70% relative WER reduction for their audio-visual model compared with its audio-only counterpart.
entries.condition: Across tested noise types and SNRs; exact aggregation varies by noise type and SNR according to the paper.

entries.text: Averaged over pretraining configurations, AVSR reduces noisy-condition WER versus audio-only ASR by 53.0% (42.6% to 20.0%) with 30h labels and 70.8% (31.3% to 9.2%) with 433h labels.
entries.condition: LRS3 noisy settings; average over four noise types and five SNRs and across pretraining configurations; audio-only versus audio-visual; 30h and 433h label settings.

entries.text: With 433h labels, speech-noise WER averages 48.1% audio-only versus 7.7% AVSR; for the other three noise categories, the corresponding averages are 25.8% versus 9.6%.
entries.condition: LRS3 mid-resource 433h condition; averages across pretraining configurations and tested SNRs; speech noise versus the other three categories (babble, music, natural).

entries.text: AV-HuBERT pretraining versus training from scratch reduces noisy WER by 78.3% (42.9% to 9.3%) with 30h labels and 53.4% (14.8% to 6.9%) with 433h labels.
entries.condition: LRS3 audio-visual noisy N-WER, averaged over four noise types and five SNRs; comparison of AV, PT=Clean with AV, PT=None in Table 3; 30h and 433h labels.
entries.quote: On average, AV-HuBERT pre-training brings substantial relative improvements of 78.3% (42.9%→9.3%) and 53.4% (14.8%→6.9%) when using 30h and 433h of labeled data,

entries.text: Noise-augmented versus clean pretraining reduces average noisy WER by 16.1% (9.3% to 7.8%) at 30h and 15.9% (6.9% to 5.8%) at 433h.
entries.condition: LRS3 audio-visual noisy N-WER averaged over four noise types and five SNRs; Table 3 clean-PT versus noisy-PT; 30h and 433h labels.
entries.quote: The WER is reduced by 16.1% (9.3%→7.8%) / 15.9% (6.9%→5.8%) on average

entries.text: Noise-augmented pretraining versus audio-visual training from scratch reduces noisy WER by 81.8% (42.9% to 7.8%) at 30h and 60.8% (14.8% to 5.8%) at 433h.
entries.condition: LRS3 audio-visual noisy N-WER averaged over four noise types and five SNRs; scratch versus noise-augmented pretraining; 30h and 433h labels.

entries.text: The authors say the gain from noise-augmented pretraining peaks around the 0dB training SNR.
entries.condition: Relative to training from scratch; qualitative claim based on Figure 2.

entries.text: AVSR outperforms audio-only ASR across noise/SNR settings except when trained from scratch with only 30h of labels.
entries.condition: Comparative claim covers tested SNR and noise types; stated exception is 30h labeled data with no pretraining.

entries.text: The authors interpret the paired visual stream as enabling effective audio-source separation in overlapping speech noise.
entries.condition: Interpretation of the speech-noise results; the paper frames it as a suggestion from the observed WERs.

entries.text: The authors leave application in real-world low-resource noisy settings to future work; the reported experiments are benchmark/noise simulations.
entries.condition: Deployment/generalization caveat; no real-world deployment results are reported.
entries.quote: applying audio-visual speech recognition in real-world low-resource noisy settings (e.g., [27]).

entries.text: The authors concede a potential domain mismatch between MUSAN babble used for training and LRS3-synthesized babble used at test time.
entries.condition: Training babble source MUSAN; test babble synthesized from LRS3; authors state the mismatch is potential.
entries.quote: which has potential domain mismatch from the babble noise synthesized from LRS3 used at test time;

entries.text: The authors could not obtain the restricted-access LRS2 audio used by Afouras et al. [14].
entries.condition: Baseline reproduction/comparability caveat for reference [14].
entries.quote: [14] uses audios from LRS2 [14], which has restricted access and we are unable to obtain it.

entries.text: The paper describes WavLM utterance mixing as requiring less than 50% intersection between secondary and primary utterances; the authors say their visual stream permits less constrained mixing.
entries.condition: Prior audio-only WavLM utterance-mixing method, as characterized by this paper; not the target model's test condition.

entries.text: LRS3 contains around 433 hours of audio-visual speech from over 5,000 speakers.
entries.condition: Full LRS3 dataset described in the paper; these are not test-split-specific counts.
entries.quote: Our experiments are conducted on LRS3 [16] with around 433 hours of audio-visual speech from over 5000 speakers,

entries.text: VoxCeleb2 has around 2,442 hours of video from over 6,000 speakers and is used for self-supervised pretraining.
entries.condition: VoxCeleb2 full collection as described; multilingual source corpus before English filtering.

entries.text: The selected English portion of VoxCeleb2 amounts to 1,326 hours of video for pretraining.
entries.condition: English-filtered VoxCeleb2 portion selected using preprocessing from [18].
entries.quote: We follow the preprocessing steps in [18] to select the ”English” portion, which amounts to 1,326 hours of videos.

entries.text: Training noise pool durations are natural 6h, music 35h, babble 20h, and speech 50h.
entries.condition: Noise training partition; categories in Table 1; natural/music/babble from MUSAN and speech from LRS3.

entries.text: Validation noise pool durations are natural 1h, music 4h, babble 2h, and speech 6h.
entries.condition: Noise validation partition; categories in Table 1.
entries.quote: validation 1 4 2 6

entries.text: Test noise pool durations are natural 1h, music 4h, babble 2h, and speech 6h.
entries.condition: Noise test partition; categories in Table 1.

entries.text: Fine-tuning uses low-resource 30h and mid-resource 433h labeled LRS3 videos.
entries.condition: LRS3 fine-tuning data settings; the paper identifies 30h and 433h as low- and mid-resource respectively.
entries.quote: using 30h of la- beled videos and a mid-resource setting using 433h of labels.

entries.text: The default AV-HuBERT LARGE encoder has 24 transformer blocks, 16 attention heads per block, and 1024/4096 embedding/feedforward dimensions.
entries.unit: blocks; heads per block; embedding/feedforward dimensions
entries.condition: Default LARGE architecture unless otherwise stated; used across experiments.
entries.quote: The model has 24 transformer blocks, where each block has 16 attention heads and 1024/4096 embedding/feedforward dimensions.

entries.text: Fine-tuning adds a randomly initialized 9-layer Transformer decoder with dimensions similar to the encoder.
entries.condition: Sequence-to-sequence AVSR decoder; paper says it has similar embedding/feedforward dimensions to the encoder.

entries.text: During training, one noise category is selected and a clip from its training partition is mixed at 0dB SNR with probability 0.25.
entries.condition: Noise augmentation in training; one selected category/clip per sample; paper says default is noise in both pretraining and fine-tuning.
entries.quote: We randomly mix the sampled noise at 0dB SNR with a probability of 0.25, following [15].

entries.text: Noisy evaluation adds each noise type at five SNR levels: -10, -5, 0, 5, and 10dB; performance on the original clean test set is also reported.
entries.condition: Separate evaluation by noise type; original clean test condition reported alongside noisy results.
entries.quote: The testing noise clips are added at five SNR levels: {−10, −5, 0, 5, 10}dB.

entries.text: By default, noise is added in both pretraining and fine-tuning.
entries.condition: Default experimental setup unless otherwise specified.
entries.quote: noise clips are added during both pre-training and finetun- ing.

entries.text: The training pipeline runs five iterations, uses BASE in all but the final iteration, and uses LARGE for the final iteration.
entries.value: 5 iterations; BASE for iterations 1-4; LARGE for iteration 5
entries.condition: AV-HuBERT pretraining pipeline; LARGE is used only in the last iteration.

entries.text: Training batches are limited to 1,000 image frames per GPU; pretraining uses 600K steps on 64 V100 GPUs, and fine-tuning uses 30K/100K steps for 30h/433h settings.
entries.unit: frames per GPU; steps; GPUs; steps
entries.condition: Reported training budget; 30K steps corresponds to 30h labels and 100K to 433h labels.

entries.text: The paper names the LRS3 dataset and says test-set results are evaluated, but does not report the number of test utterances or test speakers, nor the test-speaker overlap with training/validation speakers.
entries.condition: Evaluation-population detail; the paper reports only full-dataset scale (>5,000 speakers), not split-specific counts or overlap.
entries.quote: Our experiments are conducted on LRS3 [16] with around 433 hours of audio-visual speech from over 5000 speakers,

entries.text: The paper does not specify the LRS3 session count or a session-level train/test separation protocol.
entries.condition: Evaluation split detail; no session-based evaluation protocol is described.

entries.text: The paper does not report random seeds or repeated-run count/variance for the reported results.
entries.condition: Training and evaluation reproducibility; no mean/standard deviation or multi-seed protocol is stated in the paper.
entries.quote: The model is pre-trained with 600K steps using 64 V100-GPUs and finetuned for 30K/100K steps respectively in 30h/433h setting.

entries.text: The paper does not identify which validation data or metric selects the fine-tuned checkpoint; Table 1 describes validation noise-pool durations but not model-selection data.
entries.condition: Model selection; distinct from the noise validation durations reported in Table 1.

entries.text: The paper does not state whether audio waveform mean/variance normalization is applied or give its parameters.
entries.condition: Input preprocessing for training/evaluation; paper refers to preprocessing [18] but does not specify waveform normalization here.

entries.text: The paper identifies a sequence-to-sequence Transformer decoder but does not state the subword vocabulary/tokenizer or its size.
entries.condition: Output tokenization used in fine-tuning and evaluation.

entries.text: The paper does not report decoding beam size or length penalty.
entries.condition: Inference-time decoding configuration; distinct from the learned sequence-to-sequence decoder.

entries.text: The paper reports WER but gives no chance-level baseline or explicit null-performance criterion.
entries.condition: Metric interpretation; WER results and comparative systems are reported without a chance-level reference.

entries.text: The published pretraining and fine-tuning configurations set the random seed to 1337.
entries.condition: Repository configurations; the paper does not state this seed or establish repeated runs.
entries.quote: five iterations in total.

entries.text: Fine-tuning configurations set task.normalize=true; the task documentation defines this option as normalizing input to zero mean and unit variance.
entries.condition: Audio input normalization; this setting is omitted from the paper text.

entries.text: The repository constructs 30h data from LRS3 trainval and 433h data from non-validation LRS3 pretrain plus trainval; held-out IDs listed in lrs3-valid.id form validation. Fine-tuning uses valid and keeps the checkpoint maximizing accuracy.
entries.condition: Repository data-preparation and fine-tuning configs; the paper does not identify these IDs or the selection metric.
entries.quote: We follow the protocol of [18] to create two settings for finetuning the model;

entries.text: The repository's default LRS3 tokenizer is SentencePiece unigram with vocabulary size 1,000; fine-tuning config names sentencepiece explicitly.
entries.condition: Repository preparation default; paper does not state tokenizer type or vocabulary size.

entries.text: The default sequence-to-sequence decoder uses beam size 50 and length penalty 1.0.
entries.condition: Repository default s2s_decode.yaml; paper does not specify decoding hyperparameters.

entries.text: The repository's Seq2Seq evaluation command selects dataset.gen_subset=test; preparation maps the LRS3 test folder to that split.
entries.condition: Repository evaluation/preparation default; the paper calls it the test set but does not specify the split mapping.

entries.text: The LRS3 babble-noise preparation samples 30 clips longer than 15s from the LRS3 433h training manifest, truncates them to the shortest clip, and averages them; NumPy permutation has no fixed seed, and valid/test manifests point to the same generated babble file.
entries.value: 30 clips; >15s each; 16kHz; random permutation without script seed
entries.condition: Repository test-babble preparation; the paper reports 30 LRS3 clips but omits source manifest, duration threshold, mixing rule, and random seed.
entries.quote: 30 audio clips from LRS32 for evaluation.

entries.text: Repository noise preparation splits MUSAN speech speakers into train/valid/test groups at 80%/10%/remainder and mixes 30 speech clips per babble example; mixture counts are 8,000/1,000/1,000 with each mixture seeded by its index. Music/noise clips are randomly split 80%/10%/10%.
entries.condition: Repository MUSAN noise preparation; paper names MUSAN and reports durations but omits these generation/split details.

entries.text: Repository LRS3 speech-noise generation keeps source clips longer than 20s and divides them into train/valid/test lists at 60%/20%/20% by list order, without grouping the split by speaker; paper does not state this construction. The paper (Sec. 3.1) states no speaker overlap among noise partitions; the LRS3 speech-noise split in code is not grouped by speaker.
entries.condition: LRS3 overlapping-speech noise preparation; these are noise clips, not the target evaluation utterance split.
entries.quote: The noise audio clips in the categories of ”natural”, ”music” and ”babble” are sampled from MUSAN dataset [24], while the overlapping ”speech” noise samples are drawn from LRS3.

questions.q: What is the headline low-label babble-noise result against the prior state of the art?
questions.answer: With 30h labels, the reported five-SNR average is 14.1% WER versus 28.0% for Xu et al. [15], a 49.6% relative reduction; at 0dB, the paper reports 8.3% versus 25.5%.

questions.q: What novelty and robustness claims do the authors make?
questions.answer: They claim a first AVSR attempt using a large volume of unlabeled audio-visual speech, a new state of the art, and robustness across noise categories; the first-attempt and state-of-the-art statements are author claims, not independently established here.

questions.q: What are the main factors associated with improved noisy-condition performance?
questions.answer: The paper attributes gains to AV-HuBERT pretraining, noise-augmented pretraining, and the visual stream; it reports reductions versus scratch and audio-only systems, while identifying speech-noise separation as an interpretation of the results.

questions.q: Which evaluation details are missing from the paper, and what does the repository add?
questions.answer: The paper omits split-specific speaker/utterance counts and overlap, seed/repetition reporting, checkpoint-selection metric, input normalization, vocabulary, decoding settings, and a chance-level baseline. The linked code specifies seed 1337, normalization, validation selection by accuracy, SentencePiece vocabulary size 1,000, beam 50/length penalty 1.0/LM weight 0, and test split mapping; it does not establish speaker overlap or repeated-run results.

questions.q: What caveats do the authors acknowledge about comparison and deployment?
questions.answer: They note possible domain mismatch between MUSAN training babble and LRS3 test babble, could not obtain the restricted LRS2 audio used by Afouras et al., and leave real-world low-resource noisy deployment to future work.
